paragraphs: Let us examine whether this position is correct. I think people will agree that, as far as we know, no country has ever existed where life was so pure and simple, and food so plentiful, that nothing at all prevented early marriages. Among the lower classes, people feared that they could not support their families. Among the higher classes, people feared losing their social position. So in no country we have known has the power of population been completely free to act.

Whether a law of marriage exists or not, nature and virtue both seem to tell a man to attach himself to one woman early in life. Suppose people were free to change partners after an unhappy choice. This freedom would not affect population until it became extremely immoral. And we are now imagining a society where vice is almost unknown.

Imagine, then, a society of great equality and virtue, with pure and simple habits. Food is so plentiful that nobody fears being unable to provide well for a family. In such a society, the power of population would act without any limits. The human species would clearly increase much faster than it has ever increased before.

In the United States of America, people have had more food than in any modern European country. Their habits have been purer, and so there have been fewer obstacles to early marriage. There, the population has been found to double in twenty-five years.

This rate of growth is lower than the greatest possible power of population. But it comes from real experience, so we will take it as our rule. We will say that population, when nothing limits it, doubles every twenty-five years. In other words, it increases in a geometrical ratio.
Now let us take any piece of land, for example this Island, and see how fast the food it produces could increase. We will start with its present state of farming.

Suppose the best possible policy, with more land being farmed and strong support for agriculture. Then the produce of this Island might double in the first twenty-five years. I think this is as much as anyone can reasonably ask.

In the next twenty-five years, it is impossible to believe that the produce could become four times larger. That would go against everything we know about land. The most we can imagine is that the increase in the second twenty-five years might equal the present produce. Let us take this as our rule, even though it is surely far above the truth. Let us accept that, with great effort, the total produce of the Island might increase every twenty-five years by an amount equal to what it produces today. Even the most enthusiastic dreamer cannot imagine a greater increase. In a few centuries, it would turn every acre of land on the Island into a garden.
